title: Which faces cover a prism?
purpose: Determine rectangular and right-triangular prism surface areas from faces/nets.
knowledge: A closed prism surface includes its two ends and all lateral faces.
skills: Inventory faces,interpret a net and calculate square units.
inquiry: Does adding the edge lengths measure covering material?
story: A packaging team starts by naming every face before choosing a formula.
phases: Predict whether edge total or face areas would estimate a covering.
Ask learners to shade a face and mark an edge;retain the initial claim.
Prediction distinguishes length from area.
Complete SV1 for both prisms using the supplied schematic nets.
Allow10 minutes face inventories/calculations and6 checking;dimensions govern,not measuring the print.
Rectangular158 cm²;triangular132 cm² with two6 cm² ends.
Explain how each term corresponds to an exposed face.
Trace the triangle perimeter into the three lateral rectangles;reject omitted end faces.
Each learner can identify a missing/double-counted face in a peer inventory.
Add questions about triangular faces meeting at an apex.
Keep height/slant questions for the pyramid task.
Question names a length needed to calculate a face area.
Build a solid→exposed faces→areas→sum→unit/check model.
Collect an individual labelled inventory and one dimension check.
Exit:explain why perimeter alone cannot give the required surface area.

summary.observed: A net separates faces that cover the solid.
summary.learned: Surface area sums exposed face areas in square units.
summary.explained: A triangular prism needs its two triangular ends plus three rectangles.

Explain why the5 cm face altitude is not an apex-to-corner edge.
Use the net altitude and central section;the corner edge can be an extension√34.
Individual reasoning identifies the plane in which the altitude is perpendicular.
Add questions about curved faces and slant heights.
Keep cone unrolling separate from pyramid faces.
Learner asks which cone length corresponds to its curved surface.
Annotate the reference model with solid height/face altitude/edge distinctions.
Collect one corrected counterexample and total-area check.
Exit:state exactly what the square base contributes.

summary.observed: A pyramid face has a different altitude from the solid’s vertical height.
summary.learned: Face triangles use slant altitude;the base area must also be counted.
summary.explained: Four15 cm² faces plus36 cm² base give96 cm².

title: Can a sphere have the same kind of net?

summary.learned: Surface scaling is quadratic in radius.
summary.explained: Flat-strip approximations do not provide an exact sphere net or proof.

skills: Compute cubic units,convert litres and state data limits.
inquiry: Can outside measurements alone establish usable capacity?

Collect an individual internal-dimension explanation and reverse conversion.

summary.learned: Right-prism volume uses cross-section area×perpendicular length.
summary.explained: The3 L capacity follows from internal dimensions,not an external label alone.

title: How much does a cone or pyramid hold?
purpose: Use the one-third model and evaluate an actual/printed comparison honestly.
knowledge: Cone/pyramid volume uses base area and perpendicular height;one comparison is not a universal proof.
skills: Calculate volumes,compare matching solids and record real actions.
inquiry: What must match for a one-third comparison to be meaningful?
story: The team compares pointed and straight-sided vessels.
phases: Predict which dimensions must match in the cone/cylinder comparison.
Show prepared safe models or printed descriptions;ask for internal base and perpendicular height.
Prediction avoids substituting slant height.
Calculate SV8 cone/pyramid volumes,then use the prepared demonstration or printed ratio.
Allow8 minutes calculations,5 supervised observation/printed comparison and3 recording. Use water only with prechecked stable nonbreakable vessels/tray.
12π cone,48 pyramid;matching cylinder/prism volumes36π/144;printed ratio3. Record actual actions or not observed.
Explain how the comparison supports but does not prove the general formula.
State the mathematical one-third model and limitations of fill precision,spills and one pair of objects.
Individual reasoning separates a volume calculation from demonstrated measuring/pouring skill.
Add questions about removing a pointed top.
Keep similar-cone heights ready for the frustum task.
Learner identifies why the removed cone’s height matters.
Add pointed-solid volume formula and an honest evidence-status record.
Collect individual calculations plus observed/prompted/not-observed practical evidence.
Exit:explain why a pyramid’s face altitude is not its volume height.

summary.observed: Matching ideal cone/cylinder and pyramid/prism pairs have a1:3 volume model.
summary.learned: Use one third of base area×perpendicular height for cone/pyramid volume.
summary.explained: A practical/printed comparison illustrates the model without proving it universally.

safety: Teacher-prepared stable plastic vessels,clean water and spill tray only;no unsealed paper pouring,cutting unknown containers or substances. Keep water/electricity apart and wipe spills. Print route is valid analysis but not observed practical competence.
